value.overview: The Slate-headed Tody-Flycatcher is a tiny, compact tyrant flycatcher of tropical lowlands and foothills. It is usually found in dense vegetation along forest edges, secondary growth, scrub, clearings, and gallery forest. The species often remains inconspicuous among leaves, where it makes short flights to capture small arthropods. Its broad distribution is divided between Middle America and northern South America, with Costa Rica forming part of its resident Central American range.
value.classification: The Slate-headed Tody-Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Poecilotriccus. Its scientific name is Poecilotriccus sylvia.
value.identification: This is a very small, short-tailed flycatcher with a relatively large head and a broad, flattened bill. The head and upperparts are mainly slate-gray to olive-gray, while the underparts are generally pale yellowish or buff, with a lighter throat. It can be difficult to see because it moves through dense foliage near the ground. In Costa Rica, its subdued colors and compact shape help separate it from brighter or more boldly marked tody-flycatchers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range. In Middle America it occurs from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama; separate populations occur in northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident, occurring on both slopes but reported especially from the Pacific slope from the Gulf of Nicoya southward, with additional records in Caribbean lowlands and foothills. It uses tropical evergreen and deciduous forest edges, gallery forest, secondary forest, scrub, overgrown clearings, and open woodland, generally from sea level to about 1,000 meters.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals are expected to remain within the country throughout the year, although local movements may follow food availability or breeding conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is incomplete and varies geographically. The breeding season overall appears to extend mainly from January through August, but the timing in Costa Rica is not precisely defined. The nest is a pear-shaped structure with a side entrance, made from moss, grasses, and other plant fibers. It is usually suspended from the tip of a branch, often with some overhead cover, and generally placed within about three meters of the ground. A typical clutch contains two creamy white eggs marked with brown spots.
value.dietFeeding: The Slate-headed Tody-Flycatcher feeds mainly on small arthropods, including insects and other invertebrates, and may also take some fruit. It usually searches dense vegetation near the ground, picking prey from leaves and twigs or making short sallies from a perch. It sometimes forages higher in the vegetation, including the forest canopy, but most feeding activity occurs in shaded, leafy cover.
value.behavior: This species is generally quiet and inconspicuous, although its short calls can help reveal its presence. It commonly forages in pairs and only rarely joins mixed-species feeding flocks. The bird makes short, deliberate movements through dense foliage and may show brief tail movements while feeding. Because it often stays inside vegetation rather than perching in the open, careful observation and attention to calls are useful for detecting it in Costa Rica.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.
